notes.body_html: Hoshea 14:5: the climactic verse of the prophet’s call to teshuvah (ch. 14, “Shuvah Yisrael,” read as the haftarah of Shabbos Shuvah): “אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבָתָם, אֹהֲבֵם נְדָבָה, כִּי שָׁב אַפִּי מִמֶּנּוּ” — “I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely, for My anger has turned away from him.” Rashi (from Tanchuma, Ekev): “once they say [the words of teshuvah] before Me, I will heal their backsliding [meshuvah] and love them with a generous spirit — though they are not worthy of the love, I will freely bestow it — for My anger has turned from them.” R’ Tzadok adduces this as the source that the “healing” of which the Gemara speaks (Yoma 86a, “great is teshuvah, for it brings healing”) is the healing of forgiveness: “meshuvah” means backsliding [sin], and it is precisely this that is “healed.” Chassidic parallels — the verse itself becomes a map of the first movement of teshuvah. Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Prophets, Hoshea 14:1, reads the whole passage beginning "Ashur lo yoshienu" as Israel's surrender of every claim to spiritual self-sufficiency. Good deeds, zerizus, yirah, and even fiery ahavah are not things in which a person can finally boast; the decisive point is the "kol demamah dakah," the quiet Divine seal in the heart that the present movement truly accords with Hashem's will. The Divine response is then precisely, "ארפא משובתם אוהבם נדבה כי שב אפי ממנו" — "I will heal their backsliding... for My anger has turned from him," which the Mei HaShiloach explains as the removal of Divine anger from Israel. This fits R' Tzadok's insistence that the first refuah is the refuah of selichah: before the past has been transformed, the relationship has already been reopened and the anger has turned away. Sefas Emes, Rosh HaShanah 25:4, develops the next words, "אוהבם נדבה." There is an ahavah dependent upon conduct, which can be obscured when conduct fails, and there is the essential love of Israel because "chelek Hashem amo," an ahavah she-einah teluyah badavar. Sin can conceal the soul's revelation, but teshuvah reawakens it; hence "ארפא משובתם" is followed by "אוהבם נדבה." In the language of the Sefas Emes, the healing is not merely the cancellation of a punishment but the re-emergence of the neshama-level bond that the aveirah had hidden. This supplies a Chassidic basis for R' Tzadok's distinction between a wound that has been healed and the deeper root that was never destroyed. Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 39 (39:19 in Sefaria's segmentation), explicitly invokes the same ma'amar, "teshuvah brings healing to the world," in a strikingly concrete way: Torah learned with an ulterior motive can be held temporarily in exile within kelipas nogah, "עד אשר יעשה תשובה שמביאה רפואה לעולם, שבשובו אל ה' גם תורתו שבה עמו" — until he does teshuvah, which brings healing to the world; when he returns to Hashem, his Torah returns with him. The "world" healed by teshuvah thus includes the person's own earlier Torah and avodah: acts that were spiritually displaced are drawn back with the returning person. This is already a bridge from the first rung — healing from now on — toward the later rungs in which the past itself is recovered.

notes.body_html: Yoma 86a: “R’ Chama b’Rabbi Chanina said: Great is teshuvah, for it brings healing to the world, as it says, ‘I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely’ (Hoshea 14:5).” He further contrasts “Return, backsliding children” (implying they were always wayward — teshuvah from love, which makes the very origin as innocent) with “I will heal your backslidings” (implying, as Rashi explains, one healed like a cured baal mum of whom “a trace of his name remains” — teshuvah from fear).

notes.body_html: Maharsha, Chiddushei Aggados, Yoma 86a: questions why the Gemara did not prove that teshuvah brings healing “to the world” from “and he shall return and be healed to him” (Yeshayah 6:10), and suggests the verse speaks of literal healing, implying the sinner is not yet forgiven. R’ Tzadok rejects this: the Gemara in Megillah makes explicit that the “healing” here is forgiveness itself, which comes immediately upon teshuvah — the sinner is at once forgiven.

notes.body_html: Tehillim 103:3: “הַסֹּלֵחַ לְכָל עֲוֺנֵכִי, הָרֹפֵא לְכָל תַּחֲלֻאָיְכִי” — “Who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases” — from David’s psalm blessing Hashem for His benefactions to the soul. The two clauses run parallel — forgiveness of sin and healing of affliction — and the Gemara (Megillah 17b) derives from their order that the “healing” follows upon the “forgiveness”: first the iniquity is pardoned, then the ailments are healed. R’ Tzadok draws on this to explain the plural “refu’os [healings]” in the Gemara’s text as two — the healing of the soul (forgiveness) and the healing of the body — “for the one depends on the other,” the bodily ailments of Israel corresponding exactly to the ailments of the soul.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Dover Tzedek, Eruvin §4): “As it says in the first chapter of Kiddushin (40a), that a good thought the Holy One joins to the deed — even if he [merely] thought [to do a mitzvah] and was prevented by circumstance, Scripture reckons it for him as though he did it; but an evil thought is not joined to the deed, for the transgression is only in the deed, and it is bounded, like this world, the world of action, whereas thought has no bound or limit at all.” The se’if’s point precisely: the mere thought of teshuvah makes one “a complete tzaddik” at once — for thought reaches beyond the bounded world of deed.

notes.body_html: Kiddushin 49b: “[If a man betroths a woman] ‘on condition that I am a righteous man’ — even a completely wicked man — she is betrothed, for perhaps he had a thought of teshuvah in his mind.” R’ Tzadok adduces this as proof that a mere thought of teshuvah instantly renders one a “complete tzaddik,” even before any of the labors of rectification. Tanya and Izhbitz on the instantaneous halachic force of hirhur teshuvah. Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah ch. 1 (1:7 in Sefaria's segmentation), defines the Torah's core mitzvah of teshuvah as "עזיבת החטא בלבד" — abandoning the sin — meaning that one "יגמור בלבו בלב שלם לבל ישוב עוד לכסלה," resolves wholeheartedly in his heart not to return to rebellion against His kingship. That formulation is especially apt here: Kiddushin 49b does not require that the man's biography already be visibly rewritten; the relevant question is whether, at that moment, the heart has truly turned. R' Tzadok's "complete tzaddik immediately" therefore accords with the Alter Rebbe's definition of the essential act of teshuvah as a present, inward resolution, while the further avodos of remorse, confession, fasting, and rectification address other dimensions of kapparah and purification. Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Talmud, Berachos 4a:2, uses this very Kiddushin passage to describe the radical openness of human bechirah from one moment to the next. A person has, as it were, two open doors: "ברגע אחד יכול להשתנות ולהטיב דרכיו" — in a single moment he can change and improve his ways — and there is likewise an opening in the opposite direction. The Izhbitzer cites both halves of Kiddushin: "al menas she'ani tzaddik," perhaps he had a thought of teshuvah; and "al menas she'ani rasha," perhaps a dark thought entered him. The point is not to minimize deeds but to insist that the living point of choice is never frozen by yesterday's identity. This sharpens R' Tzadok's first rung of refuah: the past may still bear a scar, but the person's present spiritual status can turn immediately because the inner point of bechirah is alive now.

notes.body_html: Yevamos 48b: “R’ Yosei says: A convert who converts is like a newborn child [and is not punished for what preceded]. Then why are converts afflicted? notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §41): “A convert who converts is like a newborn (Yevamos 22a), and it effects that the past is forgotten and as though it is not; but they cannot rectify [it so] that the past too be good — for the root of the nations has no good in it, and the [only] good in it is that it transforms to be called by the name ‘Israel,’ and the name of the [former] nations is submerged from him. But the name ‘Israel’ is called upon even the most wicked in the world.” Exactly the se’if’s distinction: the convert’s “delay” is a root-deficiency that is never truly healed, for the past cannot be made good — unlike a born Jew, whose root is good. Further Chassidic background to "ger shenisgayer ke-katan shenolad." Kedushas Levi, Lech Lecha §37, takes the halachic principle with great literalness in explaining Avraham's break with Terach: the convert's former genealogical life no longer defines his spiritual identity; he is reborn into a new relation to Hashem. Sefas Emes, Vayera 12:3, similarly says that after the milah Avraham became "בריה חדשה כענין גר שנתגייר כקטן שנולד" — a new creature, like a convert who is as a newborn — and reads the new appearance of Hashem at the tent as the opening of an entirely new derech. Beis Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sarah 24:1, adds an Ishbitz-Radzin nuance especially relevant to R' Tzadok's language of changing the former state. After the Akeidah, milah, and the ten nisyonos, Avraham was "נשתנה מהיפך להיפך, כענין גר שנתגייר" — changed from one opposite to the other, like a convert who must overturn an ingrained former way. Rebirth is therefore not only a juridical severance from the old past but the revelation of a newly ordered personality. At the same time, these sources help preserve R' Tzadok's distinction here. A ger can truly become a new person from this point onward, yet R' Tzadok asks a different, more radical question: can the earlier reality itself become good? Resisei Layla §41 answers that for the ger the former world can be forgotten and submerged, but not transformed into a good Jewish root that was already present there. Shem MiShmuel, Shabbos Shuvah 3:12, compares the highest teshuvah to total immersion: when all the powers of the soul are swallowed into teshuvah one becomes "כקטן שנולד"; this is precisely why the analogy is so powerful for R' Tzadok — ordinary rebirth means a new beginning, whereas the higher Jewish power of teshuvah can ultimately go beyond beginning anew and recast the past itself.

notes.body_html: Bava Metzia 58b: the Mishnah (Bava Metzia 4:10), having taught that “just as there is ona’ah [wronging] in buying and selling, so is there ona’ah in words,” rules: “if one is a baal teshuvah, one may not say to him, ‘remember your former deeds.’” R’ Tzadok notes that this clause — unlike the warning against wronging the convert — is not the Torah’s own prohibition (for from the side of absolute truth a Jew’s sin is not of his essence, and no true “wronging” applies); the Sages added it, because at the beginning of teshuvah the rectification of the past is not yet manifest. The same daf continues (Bava Metzia 58b–59a): “whoever whitens the face of his fellow in public is as though he sheds blood” — Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak observing, “we see that the red departs [azil sumka] and pallor comes.” This is R’ Tzadok’s source for reading the “whitening of the face” as the departing of the red, i.e. of the blood — “the blood is the soul,” the animal soul that is the seat of sin — so that at the mention of an as-yet-unrectified sin the penitent’s blood is “swallowed within him.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §158): “Through mesirus nefesh unto death in one’s very thought, in complete truth — that he consents in his heart that if it be God’s will and better for him to die, he desires it willingly — he is saved from the decree of death… for his thought and his acceptance upon himself is reckoned as the deed itself, and it is thereafter as though he had come in a second gilgul to this world, knowing what he had spoiled in the first, and able to rectify it; and there is no sin [that cannot thus be mended].” This is the very mechanism of §1-3’s higher rung — “the root of Israel that can change even the past”: the wholehearted giving-over of the nefesh (the “blood” that is the nefesh) sets a man, as it were, in a new life over against his old, from which he can reach back and heal what was.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §164): “In the reckoning of people the baal teshuvah is not [seen] as a complete tzaddik… because teshuvah is called ‘alma de-iskasya’ [the concealed world], and its preciousness and beauty are not revealed to people” — even though the Sages taught, “in the place where baalei teshuvah stand [the wholly righteous cannot stand]” (Berachos 34b). He likens it to Leah, who “was hated” and wept — the hidden secret of teshuvah — against Rachel of “revealed beauty”; yet the essential offspring are from Leah, “for the essence of birth, the renewal of Torah and of souls by God’s will, is all through the rung of teshuvah.” This illuminates why David’s face was whitened at the mention of his sin, and why the higher rung — full rectification of the past, with no shame at all — “was not yet revealed in his lifetime”: teshuvah’s beauty belongs to the concealed world. Izhbitz-Radzin parallel to Leah as alma d'iskasya. Beis Yaakov on Torah, Vayetzei 63:1, explicitly describes the zivug of Yaakov and Leah as "עלמא דאתכסיא," above ordinary human grasp. Rachel's beauty and the stature of her children are visible on the surface; Leah and her children repeatedly require later birur. Yehudah and Tamar, Reuven and Bilhah, and other episodes can look compromised at the moment of occurrence while their inner place in the Divine plan emerges only later. That is exactly the phenomenology R' Tzadok assigns to teshuvah: its "yofi" is concealed because the present observer still sees the broken history, whereas the deeper birur by which that history becomes the vehicle of a higher birth is not yet visible. Beis Yaakov, Vayetzei 66:2, develops the same point through Leah's naming of Yehudah. On the surface she appears to have received Yehudah without the same visible struggle as the earlier children, yet "אין הקב"ה נותן בחנם רק על ידי יגיעה"; her hidden labor in the first three births is gathered into the fourth. Therefore she says "הפעם אודה את ה'," and the Midrash's "Leah grasped hoda'ah, and her children opened with hoda'ah" becomes a principle: what appeared externally unearned or even unattractive is later disclosed as the fruit of hidden avodah. R' Tzadok's equation of Leah with teshuvah is thus thoroughly Ishbitzian: the baal teshuvah belongs to a world in which the truth of a life cannot be read from its first visible form. This also explains the David connection. notes.body_html: Shmuel II 12:13: After the affair of Bas-Sheva and Uriah (Shmuel II ch. 11), the prophet Nathan came to David, told him the parable of the poor man’s ewe lamb, and declared, “You are the man!” (12:7), decreeing that “the sword shall never depart from your house” (12:10). David answered: “וַיֹּאמֶר דָּוִד אֶל־נָתָן: חָטָאתִי לַה׳. וַיֹּאמֶר נָתָן אֶל־דָּוִד: גַּם־ה׳ הֶעֱבִיר חַטָּאתְךָ, לֹא תָמוּת” — “David said to Nathan: ‘I have sinned against Hashem.’ And Nathan said to David: ‘Hashem, too, has removed your sin; you shall not die’” (Shmuel II 12:13). Radak explains that “also (gam)” comes to include David’s confession — “as you confess, so too He has accepted your teshuvah”; and “you shall not die” means “not the death of the wicked, whose soul descends to Gehinnom — though you will still be punished in this world,” namely the death of the child, Avshalom’s rebellion, and “the sword shall not depart from your house.” It is upon this instantaneous exchange — a single word of confession met at once with “Hashem has removed your sin” — that Chazal call David “the man who raised up the yoke of teshuvah” (Avodah Zarah 5a); cf. Shabbos 56a, “whoever says David sinned is merely mistaken,” and Shabbos 30a, that the full manifestation of his atonement was withheld in his lifetime. Izhbitz on David's purification. Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Writings, Tehillim 51:1, comments on David's plea "תחטאני באזוב ואטהר." He distinguishes a supernal purification in which Hashem illuminates the depth of the heart so that the person recognizes that he was bound to Him even in the hour of sin, from the more constricted purification of the ezov, given to the most distant forms of tumah. The latter requires extreme self-contraction, recognition of lowliness, and sweeping away every trace of ga'avah. David, the Mei HaShiloach says, longed so intensely for taharah that he was prepared for either path: like a man covered in filth who says to his friend, cleanse me with whatever broom you choose, only cleanse and purify me. "תחטאני באזוב" therefore expresses not self-justification but a willingness to undergo the deepest birur. That teaching is important for reading the Izhbitz-Radzin doctrine of yedi'ah and bechirah in connection with David. The higher disclosure — that even during the sin the deepest neshama had never ceased to be attached to Hashem — is a *result* of purification, not a permission granted beforehand to follow desire. Before the birur, David's avodah is confession, brokenness, and readiness for correction. Only after that can there be a revelation of a level on which the root-attachment was never severed. Shem MiShmuel repeatedly cites the Zohar on "גם ה' העביר חטאתך לא תמות" as referring to the removal of the destructive accuser generated by sin. In Nitzavim 2:15 and Sukkos 3:2-3, he explains that the sin itself creates a prosecuting force that closes the heart; through true vidui and teshuvah that force is "passed away" so the person can again turn toward Hashem. This fits R' Tzadok's exact wording of the first rung. "Hashem has removed your sin; you shall not die" is genuine and immediate healing — the death-bearing obstruction is removed — even though the later punishments in David's life show that the complete revelation of retroactive tikkun has not yet arrived.

notes.body_html: Chagigah 3a (and Bereishis Rabbah): Avraham is called “the father of converts” — the first to bring others “under the wings of the Shechinah.” R’ Tzadok: Avraham’s own starting-point was that of a ger, and only after fathering Yitzchak did he reveal his deeper root as native-born father of Israel. Avraham's transition from ger to root-father in Chassidus. Beis Yaakov, Chayei Sarah 24:1, portrays Avraham after milah, Akeidah, and the ten nisyonos as a person transformed "מהיפך להיפך" in the manner of a ger. Yet the very same transformation reveals, rather than manufactures, the depth for which he was created. This is close to R' Tzadok's paradox: Avraham begins historically as the first ger, but after Yitzchak is included in him the earlier stage itself can be read from the standpoint of his native root as father of Israel. Kedushas Levi, Lech Lecha §37, similarly refuses to define Avraham by Terach. Using "ger shenisgayer ke-katan shenolad," he argues that Avraham's true av is the Divine middah and mission from which he is spiritually hewn — the revelation of Hashem's Name through the future Jewish people. Thus the ger-principle becomes not simply erasure of ancestry but discovery of a deeper ancestry. R' Tzadok pushes this one step farther: once Yitzchak and Yaakov are understood as already latent in Avraham, the branch discloses what was hidden in the root, and the past can be reread accordingly.

notes.body_html: Tehillim 110:3: “עַמְּךָ נְדָבֹת בְּיוֹם חֵילֶךָ, בְּהַדְרֵי קֹדֶשׁ מֵרֶחֶם מִשְׁחָר, לְךָ טַל יַלְדֻתֶיךָ” — a verse whose plain meaning is famously difficult. Rashi reads the psalm as addressed to Avraham: “your people will volunteer on the day of your host” — when Avraham mustered his men to pursue the four kings (Bereishis 14), Aner, Eshkol, and Mamre going out with him of their own accord; “in the beauty of holiness, from the womb” — in the merit of the holiness that was in him from his mother’s womb, for “he recognized his Creator at the age of three” (Nedarim 32a); and “yours is the dew of your youth [lecha tal yaldusecha]” — “your youth shall be reckoned to you: the ways of uprightness by which you conducted yourself in your youth will be to you as pleasant as this dew.” R’ Tzadok links this to the Midrash (Bereishis Rabbah 39) that Avraham feared, “shall I say that there is sin in my hand?” and was reassured that he is “the beloved of the world [meruchamo shel olam]”: Avraham was in truth holy from the womb, so that his beginning as a convert — the “youth” preceding the revealing of his root — is itself like dew, pure and pleasant, and no taint.

notes.body_html: Yirmeyah 50:20: “בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם וּבָעֵת הַהִיא נְאֻם ה׳, יְבֻקַּשׁ אֶת עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ, וְאֶת חַטֹּאת יְהוּדָה וְלֹא תִמָּצֶאינָה, כִּי אֶסְלַח לַאֲשֶׁר אַשְׁאִיר” — “In those days and at that time, says Hashem, the iniquity of Israel shall be sought and there shall be none, and the sins of Judah and none shall be found; for I will pardon those I leave as a remnant.” The verse falls within Yirmeyah’s prophecy of the downfall of Bavel and the return of Israel (ch. 50): at that future time Israel’s sin is not merely forgiven but “sought and not found” — uprooted entirely. This is R’ Tzadok’s emblem for the highest rung of teshuvah, the rectification of the past itself. Radak explains that the verse must speak of the Messianic future — “for I will pardon” — since sinners still remained throughout the Second Temple and this present exile; and “to the remnant I leave” likewise points to that time, as in “he who remains in Zion and is left in Jerusalem shall be called holy” (Yeshayah 4:3) and “the remnant of Israel shall do no wrong” (Tzefaniah 3:13).

notes.body_html: Yerushalmi Makkos 2:6: “They asked Wisdom: what is the sinner’s punishment? It said, ‘evil pursues sinners’ (Mishlei 13:21). They asked Prophecy: ‘the soul that sins shall die’ (Yechezkel 18:4). They asked the Holy One: ‘let him do teshuvah and it will atone for him.’” — Tanchuma, Ha’azinu: “One who does teshuvah, He shows him favor — one might think for all [nations]; Scripture says ‘to you’ — and not to another nation.” R’ Tzadok marshals these (with the Ramma and Abarbanel) that the Torah’s innovation of teshuvah-that-rectifies-the-past was given to Israel alone; the nations have only “healing going forward” (as at Nineveh). Chassidic explanation of why teshuvah belongs uniquely to the root of Israel. Shem MiShmuel, Ki Seitzei 2:17, writes that the effectiveness of teshuvah for Israel is bound to their essential connection to Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov. Jewish souls are "בעצם נפשות טהורות וטובות" — intrinsically pure and good — and aveiros are a contingent soiling. When a Jew returns, the inner point reconnects with the chain reaching the Avos and a new current of life can flow from the root. This is nearly the same metaphysical distinction R' Tzadok draws here between sin that is incidental to a good shoresh and sin that belongs to an essence lacking that root. Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 2 (2:1), supplies the Chabad formulation of the same root claim: "ונפש השנית בישראל היא חלק אלוה ממעל ממש." The Divine soul of Israel is not merely an ethically improved personality but a soul whose deepest origin is Godly. On this account teshuvah can be more than behavioral correction: return is literally return to the soul's own source. R' Tzadok's language remains his own and should not be collapsed into Tanya's system, but the comparison clarifies why a Jewish past can ultimately be healed from within: the deepest subject of that past was never identical with the sin.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §54): “Whereas the nations of the world — even should they repent — ‘teshuvah was given only to Israel’ (Midrash Tanchuma Ha’azinu 4); but for them there is no atonement at all, for by them the sin is in its very essence [be-etzem].” This is the ground of §1-5’s ruling that among the nations “it is not an enduring healing, and in the end the wound is destined to reopen”: the Torah’s teshuvah was legislated for Israel alone — “whose root is truly good” — so their sins are but incidental thorns, whereas for the nations the sin cleaves to the essence itself, and even their “forward-healing” cannot hold. R’ Tzadok there rests the point, exactly as the se’if does, on the same Tanchuma: “to you — and not to another nation.”

notes.body_html: Yeshayah 60:21: “וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים, לְעוֹלָם יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ, נֵצֶר מַטָּעַי מַעֲשֵׂה יָדַי לְהִתְפָּאֵר” — “And your people, all of them righteous, shall inherit the land forever; the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, in which I take glory.” From Yeshayah’s prophecy of the future redemption of Tzion (ch. 60). R’ Tzadok cites it to contrast Israel with the nations: because at their root “your people are all righteous,” a Jew is called a complete tzaddik the instant the stirring of teshuvah begins. Rashi (on lehispa’er): “that I shall take glory in them.” And the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 90a, Perek Chelek) makes this verse the prooftext that “all Israel have a share in the World to Come, as it is said, ‘and your people are all righteous, they shall inherit the land forever.’” The phrase "ועמך כולם צדיקים" receives a striking Chassidic complement in Tanya ch. 2. If the neshama of Israel is "chelek Eloka mima'al mamash," then the prophetic designation "all of your people are righteous" can be read as a statement about root-identity rather than a denial of actual transgression. The revealed personality can become entangled in sin, while the second, Divine soul remains the inner source to which teshuvah returns. Sefas Emes, Rosh HaShanah 25:4, expresses the same distinction in terms of two loves. There is an ahavah awakened by mitzvos and good deeds, and there is the essential love of Israel rooted in "chelek Hashem amo," which is not dependent on a particular deed and cannot be extinguished by "many waters." Sin obscures the manifestation of the neshama; teshuvah causes it to awaken again. Thus R' Tzadok's use of "ועמך כולם צדיקים" is not sentimental: it is the ontological premise that allows teshuvah to uncover a righteousness deeper than the historical act.

notes.body_html: Yoma 87a: “One who seeks pardon from his fellow need not ask more than three times” (for that suffices as appeasement). notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §242): “Teshuvah is like the hataras chacham [a Sage’s release of a vow], which uproots the matter retroactively [le-mafrea], so that the evil angel formed from the sin is nullified entirely; whereas [teshuvah] from love, by which [sins] become as merits, means not that [the sin] is nullified but that it is transformed to good — and these are two rungs, le-is’hapcha [to transform] and le-ischafya [to subdue].” This lays bare precisely what §1-6’s Chesed-forgiveness lacks: Chesed only pardons a sin that still exists (hence “forward” only, and “shame remains”), whereas the higher, forceful rung uproots it from its origin — as though it had never been — which is why “to be as if he had never sinned at all is impossible when the forgiveness is from the side of Chesed.”

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §40): “The essence of teshuvah is until Hashem enlightens his eyes, that the willful sins become as merits — that he recognize and grasp that all he sinned was also by the will of Hashem” (as in Berachos 31b, and the Arizal’s reconciling of foreknowledge and free choice, “both true, each in its own domain”); “and when he attains this immense light, then all his willful sins are turned [to merits].” This is the crown of the rung §1-6 opens toward: not the Chesed that pardons yet leaves shame, but the Gevurah-born light in which the past itself is re-read as Divine guidance — the “as if he had never sinned,” and beyond. Izhbitz-Radzin on yedi'ah and bechirah — and the boundary that prevents this doctrine from becoming an excuse for sin. Mei HaShiloach, Vayeilech 3, says that even though bechirah is given into human hands, one who sees deeply recognizes that human action is "רק דבר מועט כקליפת השום" relative to the encompassing Divine conduct. In Tazria 2 he can say simultaneously that a person's eventual attainment was prepared from the beginning of creation and, nevertheless, "מצד האדם יש לו בחירה." The two statements are intentionally held together: from the creature's lived standpoint, command, responsibility, restraint, and teshuvah are real; from the later Divine illumination, the person may discover a providential depth that was never visible at the moment of choice. This is the key to R' Tzadok's use of the Arizal's yedi'ah/bechirah resolution and his statement that, at the highest teshuvah, a person can recognize that "all he sinned was also by the will of Hashem." The recognition belongs to the *afterward* of teshuvah — "until Hashem enlightens his eyes" — not to the beforehand of temptation. Mei HaShiloach, Devarim 2, sometimes reads the Torah's naming of places of Israel's sins as teaching that circumstances and spiritual "place" can radically narrow a person's field of choice. But Beis Yaakov, Bereshis 69:1, supplies the essential guardrail through its reading of Cain. Cain's "השומר אחי אנכי" is understood as the claim that overwhelming anger had removed his bechirah and therefore he should not be liable. The Divine answer rejects the self-exculpation: "קול דמי אחיך צועקים" proves that the deficiency is attributed to Cain and that he had a point of responsibility by which he could have guarded himself. The Ishbitz doctrine therefore works in two directions at once. Before and during action, a Jew must regard himself as a baal bechirah, obey Torah, resist the yetzer, and never invoke hidden providence to legitimate a prohibited act. After a genuine teshuvah that has uprooted identification with the sin, Hashem may reveal a deeper yedi'ah: the fall itself can be integrated into a providential road by which the person came to a higher recognition. That latter illumination is what R' Tzadok associates with zedonos becoming zechuyos. It does not say the aveirah was permitted; it says that Divine omnipotence can reclaim even the prohibited past and make the *teshuvah born from it* part of the final good. This is the precise Izhbitz-Radzin frame in which the radical sentence of Tzidkas HaTzadik §40 should be read.
